title: Whittled oak garden dibber
subtitle: Seasoned oak: a pointed dibber for seed and bulb planting
excerpt: A hand-whittled dibber for making planting holes. Oak is the right timber for a working garden tool, dense, hard, and slow to rot in damp soil. The point is made with long push cuts, the handle shaped for a comfortable grip, and the whole thing finished with boiled linseed oil.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the taper-point method on a round-section tool; Newey & Drage Practical Carpentry for the oak selection and finish.

glossaryTerms.definition: A short straight-bladed knife with a stout handle; the standard whittling knife for shaping and tapering.

content.text: A garden dibber is a pointed stick for making holes in soil for seeds, bulbs, and plugs. Oak is the sensible choice for a tool that goes into the ground: dense enough to push through compacted soil, and slow to rot due to its tannins. A turned dibber from a lathe takes minutes on a machine; a whittled one from an oak dowel takes the same time at a carving stool and teaches the taper-point cut used across the category.
Before you start cutting.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one, the dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.
What you need
Wood

One straight-grained oak section, 30 cm long, 25, 30 mm square or round. A short oak dowel from a timber merchant works well. Ash is a good alternative, slightly lighter, equally dense, equally rot-resistant. Hazel is acceptable for a lighter dibber used in raised-bed soil rather than compacted ground.
Tools
Sloyd knife
for shaping the point and handle.
Leather strop.
120-grit and 240-grit sandpaper.
Boiled linseed oil (BLO) for finishing, not food-safe, but correct for a garden tool. Note: oil-soaked rags spontaneously combust, spread flat to dry or submerge in water before disposal.
Workspace
A carving stool or bench. Oak is hard even when seasoned, the sloyd knife needs to be sharper than it does for green lime or hazel.
The work
Step 1: Mark the taper

Mark the point section: the bottom 12 cm of the dibber tapers from the full diameter to a blunt point (not sharp, a sharp point breaks off in use). Mark this taper line around the rod 12 cm from the point end.
Step 2: Carve the point taper
Use long
push cuts

from the taper line down toward the point tip, blade angled at about 15 degrees to the rod surface. On oak, these cuts are short, move the knife about 3 cm per stroke and then reset. The grain runs along the rod; cuts along the length are predictable. Cuts across the grain at a steep angle are not. Use
slicing cuts
, drawing the blade at an angle across the end-grain rather than pushing it straight in, to shape the very tip of the point.
Step 3: Shape the handle

The upper 18 cm is the handle. Carve a slight waist about 10 cm from the top end so the hand naturally finds the grip position. Chamfer the top end to prevent splitting. A simple groove cut around the handle 5 cm from the top gives a thumb rest.
Step 4: Sand the point
Wrap 120-grit sandpaper around the point and work along the taper. Follow with 240-grit. A smooth point glides through soil more cleanly than a rough one.
Finishing

Apply boiled linseed oil to all surfaces. Work it well into the grain, especially the end-grain at the point tip. Let dry for twenty-four hours. Repeat. BLO seals the grain against moisture penetration and extends the life of the dibber in wet soil. BLO oil-soaked rags must be laid flat to dry or submerged in water, they can smoulder if bunched up.
Variations
Depth-marked dibber: cut a series of grooves at 5 cm intervals along the shaft to show planting depth without measuring.
T-handle dibber: cut a cross-piece from the same oak and lash or peg it at right angles to the top of the shaft for a two-hand dibber for larger bulbs.
Care
Rinse off soil after use and let dry. Re-oil once a season or when the wood looks grey and dry. Keep out of prolonged standing water, even oak will eventually rot if never allowed to dry.

attrs.symptom: The knife stalls on the point taper
attrs.cause: Oak is hard and the blade needs stropping more frequently than with green wood
attrs.fix: Strop between every ten cuts on seasoned oak. If the blade still drags, switch to slicing cuts, the blade drawn at an angle reduces the effective resistance considerably on hard end-grain areas.
